title: OA Survival Kit — Harnesses, stdin I/O, and Wrappers
relevance: Real company OAs often bury an easy algorithm behind stdin parsing, fixed harnesses, and exact stdout formatting that LeetCode never trains.
company_notes: Cisco, Amazon, and D. E. Shaw OAs may use stdin/main or a locked provided harness; HackerRank, Codility, and CodeSignal commonly use function-stubs.

phases.goal: Establish how real OA wrappers differ from LeetCode method stubs and name the three harness styles.

must_hit.point: LeetCode calls a Solution method after handling I/O; many real OAs give a main that reads stdin, a provided struct/parser, or an empty file where you must read stdin and print stdout yourself.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts platform-managed function stubs with stdin/stdout or locked harness wrapping.

must_hit.point: The algorithm is usually easy; the wrapping—parsing raw text and formatting the exact expected output—is what fails under time pressure.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says the wall is I/O/format fidelity, not inventing a hard algorithm.

must_hit.point: Three harness styles: function-stub (platform I/O; HackerRank/Codility/CodeSignal), provided full harness (struct, parse_input, format_output, fill solve; Cisco style), and bare main (empty file; competitive-programming style).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all three and maps each to who owns parsing/output.

must_hit.point: Identify the wrapper type in the first 30 seconds: stub means focus on logic; bare main means paste a fast-I/O template immediately.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions early wrapper triage and different first moves per style.

probes: How does a real OA differ from a LeetCode Solution method, and what are the three harness styles you might see?
If the editor is blank versus a locked solve stub, what do you do in the first half-minute?

hints.1: Think about who reads stdin and who prints the answer.
hints.2: Map LeetCode stubs to three OA styles: stub, provided harness, bare main.
hints.3: Algorithm is easy; parsing/format wrapping is the failure mode—triage wrapper in ~30 seconds.

phases.goal: Show muscle-memory stdin idioms, the cin/getline trap, fast I/O rules, and how a provided harness is structured.

must_hit.point: cin >> reads whitespace-delimited tokens, skips leading spaces/tabs/newlines, and for string stops at the first whitespace.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes token extraction and whitespace skipping correctly.

must_hit.point: Common patterns: read N then N ints into a vector; read R and C then an R×C grid; read N vertices and M edges into an adjacency list; read T then loop T cases; or while (cin >> x) until EOF.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recalls several of these stdin shapes without inventing formats.

must_hit.point: Classic bug: cin >> n leaves a trailing newline; immediate getline reads an empty line—flush with cin.ignore up to and including '\n' (e.g. numeric_limits<streamsize>::max()).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains leftover newline and the ignore fix before getline.

must_hit.point: Fast I/O: ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false) and cin.tie(nullptr); after sync_with_stdio(false), never mix scanf/printf with cin/cout.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both desync/untie and the no-mix rule.

must_hit.point: Provided harness pieces: InputData struct, parse_input, format_output, main, and solve—edit only solve; do not touch the rest or signatures.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the pieces and states the golden rule of editing only solve.

must_hit.point: Struct fields document the input and can hint the algorithm (e.g. separate B and K in Drone imply state search); C++ solve may return a compound type while C uses out-parameter arrays filled by void solve.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions reading fields for algorithm hints and return vs out-params.

probes: Walk through reading N then an array, then explain what goes wrong if you cin >> id and immediately getline a name.
In a Cisco-style harness, what may you edit, and what do parse_input and format_output do?

hints.1: Start from cin >> token reading and the leftover-newline pitfall.
hints.2: Cover desync/untie, no mixing C I/O, then the five harness pieces.
hints.3: Only fill solve; use ignore after >> before getline; struct fields (like B vs K) hint state.

phases.goal: Contrast output and API choices that trade correctness/latency under OA constraints.

must_hit.point: std::endl inserts a newline and flushes; in a loop of 100,000 iterations that flush alone can TLE—prefer "\n".
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts endl flush cost with plain newline.

must_hit.point: For massive output, avoid calling cout hundreds of thousands of times; build a large string (optionally reserve) and dump with fputs/fwrite.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes buffered string + C-style dump vs many cout calls.

must_hit.point: C++ can return vector of pairs from solve; C often has main pre-allocate answer arrays and pass pointers as out-parameters for void solve to fill.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares return compound value vs out-parameter fills.

must_hit.point: For a FIFO bounded to 1000 tasks under tight latency: ring buffer gives true O(1) worst-case enqueue/dequeue; two-stack queue is O(1) amortized but can spike O(N) when dumping inbox to outbox.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Picks ring buffer for deadline-sensitive paths and explains the dump spike.

probes: Why prefer "\n" over endl in tight loops, and when would you buffer output for fputs?
For a latency-sensitive bounded queue, ring buffer or two-stack—and why?

hints.1: Think about flushing and how often you touch the OS write path.
hints.2: Compare endl vs \n, then many cout vs one big string dump; then return vs out-params.
hints.3: endl flushes (100,000-loop TLE risk); ring buffer O(1) worst-case beats two-stack dump spikes.

phases.goal: Apply harness literacy to real OA problems and a concrete attack checklist.

must_hit.point: Attack any OA: (1) read the struct or signature; (2) find the trivial logic behind jargon; (3) fill the stub without touching boilerplate; (4) match output character-for-character including -1 sentinels and newlines.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recites the four-step attack in order.

must_hit.point: Cisco Drone Delivery: shortest path with battery and voucher recharges—state-augmented 0-1 BFS on (row, col, battery_left, vouchers_left); adjacent moves weight 1, kiosk recharge weight 0.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names augmented state and 0-1 BFS edge weights correctly.

must_hit.point: On the 1x8 drone example with B = 4, K = 1, and kiosks at (0,1) and (0,4), expected minimum moves is 7.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States expected output 7 for that scenario or walks the recharge-then-finish path.

must_hit.point: Cisco Sniper Detector: variable sliding window over bids with a frequency map and ordered set of users at threshold K; watch long long constraints and window boundary t_i - t' <= W; dual output per line.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes window + freq + ordered set and format/type traps.

must_hit.point: 60-second checklist: identify wrapper; read input format/types; find trivial logic; write solve decoupled from parsing; match output byte-for-byte; test the provided example before submit.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Hits the checklist steps without inventing extras.

probes: How would you approach a locked Cisco harness on first open?
For Drone Delivery, why is plain (row,col) BFS wrong, and what technique replaces it?

hints.1: Start from the struct/signature, not the story text.
hints.2: Map Drone to state+0-1 BFS and Sniper to sliding window + map/set.
hints.3: Edit only solve; augment state with battery/vouchers; match -1 and newlines; run the sample.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: endl newline-flushes every time; in large loops that flush can TLE by itself—use "\n" and let the buffer flush less often.

tradeoffs.topic: Many cout calls vs string buffer + fputs/fwrite
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Huge line counts (e.g. sniper-style output) should append into one reserved string and print once with fputs/fwrite instead of hundreds of thousands of stream inserts.
Default sync/tie lets you mix C and C++ I/O safely but is slow; desync+untie is fast but forbids mixing scanf/printf with cin/cout.

tradeoffs.topic: C++ return values vs C out-parameters
tradeoffs.strong_answer: C++ solve can return vector<pair<...>>; C often uses void solve writing into caller-allocated flag/smallest arrays.

tradeoffs.topic: Ring buffer vs two-stack queue (bounded FIFO)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Ring buffer: O(1) worst-case enqueue/dequeue via modulo indexing. Two-stack: O(1) amortized but O(N) dump spikes—prefer ring buffer under tight deadlines.

gotchas.correction: Extraction leaves '\n' in the stream; getline reads an empty line—call cin.ignore(..., '\n') first.
Buffers diverge; you get jumbled/incorrect I/O—stick to one I/O family after desync.

gotchas.trap: Using endl in a hot output loop
gotchas.correction: Each endl flushes; prefer "\n" to avoid TLE from flush overhead alone.

gotchas.trap: Editing parse_input, format_output, main, struct, or signatures in a provided harness
gotchas.correction: Only implement solve; changing the rest breaks the hidden runner.
Validity depends on battery and vouchers—augment state and use 0-1 BFS (move cost 1, recharge cost 0).

gotchas.trap: Sniper window boundary or int overflow on timestamps/IDs
gotchas.correction: Keep bids with long long; enforce t_i - t' <= W; use hash map not tiny arrays; emit flag and smallest sniper per line.

gotchas.trap: Path-sum success on non-leaf when remaining equals node value
gotchas.correction: Require a leaf (no left/right) before accepting the target match.
Also drain leftover B after the main two-pointer loop.

gotchas.trap: Unsigned/signed mix, post-increment *p++, or C++ negative modulo in MCQs
gotchas.correction: a+b with unsigned promotes -20 to a huge unsigned ("Greater"); *p++ yields old value then advances; a%b keeps dividend sign (e.g. -5%3 => -2).
